The Corinthians, and his rivals, wanted a leader who looked powerful. Paul insists that the pattern of the cross governs Christian ministry.

The first chapters of the book go to great lengths to show that David did not take the throne by murder. Each person who hopes to win his favor by killing a rival (the Amalekite, Joab, Rechab and Baanah) is rebuked or executed. David waits for God and for the people. The book presents this as the mark of a true king, and it makes the later chapters, where David himself grasps what is not his, all the more shocking.

Ephesians speaks more than any other of Paul's letters about rulers, authorities, and powers in the heavenly realms. Christ has been seated far above them all (1:21), the church makes God's wisdom known to them (3:10), and believers struggle not against flesh and blood but against them (6:12). The letter takes spiritual evil seriously without making it the center: the center is Christ's victory, and the believer's task is to stand.

Praise in the Psalms is response: to God's work in creation, to his rescue of Israel, and to his help in a particular crisis. Thanksgiving psalms often retell the distress and the deliverance before the congregation, so that one person's rescue becomes the whole community's reason to worship.

Luke shows Jesus praying at the turning points of his life: at his baptism, before choosing the Twelve, before Peter's confession, at the transfiguration, in Gethsemane, and on the cross. Only Luke records the parables of the persistent friend at midnight, the persistent widow, and the Pharisee and the tax collector praying in the temple. Prayer in Luke is the ordinary posture of those who wait on God.

Nehemiah prays at length when he hears the news (chapter 1), prays in a single breath before answering the king (2:4), and sets guards while praying against attack. The book never sets prayer against planning. It treats careful work, risk, and organization as ways of trusting God.

The book ends with a request and a question: restore us, unless you have utterly rejected us (5:21-22). Scripture includes a prayer that has not yet been answered. That ending gives permission to keep praying before the answer comes, and it points beyond the book to the restoration the later prophets promise.

Edom's sin begins in the heart: "The pride of your heart has deceived you" (verse 3). Secure in its rock strongholds, confident in its wisdom and its alliances, Edom believed no one could reach it. Obadiah answers that no height is beyond God. The theme runs through the whole Bible, from the tower of Babel to Mary's song that God has brought down rulers from their thrones, and it is always a warning to the reader as well as a word about others.

Haggai's central challenge is about priorities. The people had time and resources for their own houses but not for God's. The temple was the place of God's presence and the center of Israel's worship, and neglecting it meant treating God as an afterthought. Haggai calls them to put first things first.

The first generation dies, but the promise to Abraham does not. Balaam, hired to curse, can only bless, and he declares that God is not a man who changes his mind (23:19). The second census shows a nation still numbering in the hundreds of thousands, and the closing chapters legislate for a land Israel has not yet entered. God's faithfulness, not Israel's, carries the story forward.

God swore to David that his house and kingdom would endure, and 1 Kings shows that promise holding through Solomon's accession, through the division of the kingdom, and through bad kings in Jerusalem. The reason Judah keeps a king of David's line is repeatedly said to be for David's sake. The promise is unconditional in its core and conditional in how each king experiences it, a tension the book leaves standing.

The word seed, or offspring, runs from 3:15 through the promises to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Yet the promise keeps meeting obstacles: barren wives, murdered sons, famine, a father told to sacrifice his heir, brothers who try to kill one of their own. Genesis shows that the line of promise survives because God preserves it, not because the family is strong or good.

Prophets and seers appear at nearly every turn: Shemaiah, who is also known from Kings, and many known only from Chronicles, such as Azariah son of Oded, Hanani, Jahaziel, Zechariah son of Jehoiada, Oded. They warn, encourage, and interpret events. Their presence shows that judgment never came without warning, a point the closing chapter makes explicitly: the LORD sent messengers again and again “because He had compassion on them and on His dwelling place” (36:15).

The people of Genesis lie, scheme, play favorites, and betray one another, and God works through all of it without excusing any of it. The theme comes to its clearest statement at the end, when Joseph tells his brothers that what they intended for evil God intended for good (50:20). Genesis teaches that God's plan is not derailed by human sin, which is both a comfort and a warning.

No one in Ruth sees a vision or witnesses a wonder. Famine ends, harvests come, Ruth happens to enter the field of Boaz, the nearer redeemer happens to pass by the gate. The narrator lets the reader see God's hand in these ordinary turns without forcing the point. Ruth is one of the Bible's clearest pictures of a God who governs the small events of ordinary life for his purposes.

Who should rule Israel? Gideon refuses to be king because the LORD is Israel's ruler, then lives like one. Abimelech takes the crown by murder and brings ruin. Jotham's fable mocks a king who is only a bramble. The closing refrain, that there was no king in Israel and everyone did what was right in his own eyes, points toward the need for faithful leadership under God, and the books that follow take up that longing.

The go'el, or kinsman-redeemer, was a near relative responsible for protecting a family's land, name, and people when they could not protect themselves. The word and its verb run through chapters 2 to 4. Boaz takes on the role at cost to himself, and the book shows redemption not as an abstraction but as a person acting to restore land, household, and future.

Jehoash, Hezekiah, and Josiah all attempt reform, and the book honors them. Yet it also shows that reform led from the top cannot by itself change a people's heart. Josiah's is the most thorough reform in the book, and still the judgment comes, which leaves readers looking for a deeper renewal than any king could bring.

themes.title: The reliability of the apostolic and prophetic word

entries.body: Against teachers who dismissed Christ's return as myth, 2 Peter appeals to two witnesses: the apostles who saw Christ's glory, and the prophets whose words came from God by the Spirit. The letter also places Paul's letters beside the other Scriptures, an early sign of the church recognizing its apostolic writings.

Jonah is not a hero. He runs, sleeps through the storm, preaches the shortest sermon in the prophets, and then sulks when it works. The book holds him up as a mirror to God's people, who can confess God's grace in words and resent it in practice.

Memory is one of the book's great concerns. Israel must remember that it was a slave in Egypt, that God led it through the wilderness, and that he fed it with manna. The great danger is not hardship but prosperity: when they have eaten and are satisfied in houses they did not build, they will be tempted to forget the LORD and credit themselves (8:11-18). Teaching children, reciting the law, and keeping the festivals all serve this memory.

The book closes by turning a rescue into a festival, with feasting, gifts to one another, and gifts to the poor. Remembering is itself an act of faith: each Purim retells the story so that later generations, facing their own Hamans, would know they had been preserved before.

The returnees see themselves as a remnant, the survivors God has spared. That brings gratitude and also fear, because the sins that caused the exile could return. Ezra's prayer in chapter 9 is a model of corporate confession in which the leader counts himself among the guilty.

Again and again Micah pictures God as a shepherd who gathers the lame, the outcast, and the scattered (2:12, 4:6-7, 7:14), and a coming ruler who shepherds in the LORD's strength (5:4). Judgment is not God's last word; a remnant will be gathered and restored.

The Chronicler is the Old Testament's great narrator of turning back. Rehoboam and his officials humble themselves and are spared destruction; Hezekiah invites the north to return; and Manasseh, the worst king of all in Kings, is shown in Chronicles taken captive, praying, and restored, so that “Manasseh knew that the LORD is God” (33:13). For a community that had lived through judgment, this was the heart of the message: God receives those who return.

Joel's central summons is "rend your hearts and not your garments" (Joel 2:13). Outward signs of grief such as fasting, weeping, and sackcloth are not dismissed; the prophet calls for them. But he insists that they express an inward turning back to God. Repentance in Joel is communal as well as personal: elders, priests, children, and even a bride and groom on their wedding day are called to stand before God together.

God promises rest (1:13-15), and the book reports that he gave it (21:44, 23:1). The land is Israel's inheritance, divided by lot so that every tribe and clan receives a share from God's hand. Later Scripture treats this rest as real but provisional, a foretaste of a greater rest still to come (Psalm 95, Hebrews 4).

God promises to repay the years the locusts ate, to send rain in its season, and to make his people no longer a reproach among the nations. He also holds the nations accountable for scattering his people, selling children, and looting sacred things. Restoration in Joel includes both the healing of the land and the righting of wrongs.

Parts of the church behaved as if they had already arrived, rich and reigning. Paul reminds them that the end has not come: they still wait for the revelation of Christ, the day of judgment, and the resurrection of the body. Chapter 15 grounds Christian hope in Christ's bodily resurrection and makes it the reason that labor in the Lord is not in vain.

The book opens with God's invitation, return to me and I will return to you (1:3), and the whole of it unfolds that promise. The people are to turn from the ways of their fathers; God, in turn, comes back to Jerusalem with mercy, to live among them. Zechariah insists that the exile was real judgment for real refusal (7:11-14), and that God's return is pure mercy rather than a reward earned.

The book's plot is a series of turnings upside down. Haman plans honor for himself and has to give it to Mordecai; he builds a gallows for Mordecai and dies on it; a decree of destruction is answered by a decree of defense; mourning becomes feasting. The narrator names the pattern when he says the enemies' plan was overturned (9:1). The reversals teach that the powers who seem to control history do not have the last word.

Three times the woman charges the daughters of Jerusalem not to arouse or awaken love until the time is right. Love is powerful, and the Song treats it as something to be guarded as well as enjoyed. Much of the Christian and Jewish tradition has read this as a call to patience and chastity, keeping the full expression of love for its proper setting.

Paul's theme phrase has been read in several ways: as the righteous standing God gives to believers, as God's own saving faithfulness to his promises, or as both at once. The letter shows God as just in judging sin and just in justifying the one who believes (3:26). Whatever the precise emphasis, the phrase names God acting in Christ to set things right.

The word today carries weight in Luke: today a Savior is born (2:11), today the Scripture is fulfilled (4:21), today salvation has come to Zacchaeus's house (19:9), today the thief will be with Jesus in paradise (23:43). Salvation is present, not only future. And it brings joy: the angels announce good news of great joy, and heaven rejoices over one sinner who repents (15:7).

Timothy has known the Holy Scriptures from infancy, and they can make him wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus (3:15). All Scripture is God-breathed and equips the servant of God for every good work (3:16-17). This is the New Testament's most direct statement about the nature of Scripture, and it undergirds the charge to preach the word (4:2).

The Chronicler uses a simple and searching vocabulary. To seek the LORD is to turn to him in worship, prayer, and obedience; to be unfaithful is to break faith with him, as Saul did. Seeking brings help and blessing; unfaithfulness brings disaster, as the note about Judah's exile in 1 Chronicles 9:1 shows. The pattern is not mechanical fate but an invitation, because every generation can still seek him.

The verb "seek" runs through the book as its measure of a king. To seek the LORD is to turn toward him in worship, obedience, and trust, especially in a crisis. Kings who seek him are helped; kings who forsake him are forsaken. The pattern is stated in God's reply to Solomon, “if My people who are called by My name humble themselves and pray and seek My face and turn from their wicked ways, then I will hear from heaven, forgive their sin, and heal their land” (7:14), and the rest of the book tests it reign by reign.

themes.title: The self-destruction of greed and violence

entries.body: The five woes of chapter 2 show evil undoing itself. The plunderer is plundered, the house built by violence cries out against its builder, and the idol maker trusts a lifeless thing. God's judgment often works through the consequences of sin itself.

John calls Jesus' miracles signs because they point beyond themselves. Each reveals something of his glory, the visible weight and brightness of God's presence that Israel saw in the tabernacle and temple. The signs provoke both faith and opposition, and the Gospel suggests that faith resting only on miracles is fragile. The fullest display of glory comes, paradoxically, at the cross, when the Son is lifted up.

Romans treats sin not only as wrong acts but as a power that reigns over humanity, entering through Adam and bringing death with it. That is why the answer cannot be simple self-improvement. People need to be rescued and brought under a new reign, the reign of grace.

The poems accept the prophets' verdict: Jerusalem sinned, and the LORD has done what he warned he would do (2:17). Prophets and priests are singled out for blame (2:14; 4:13). Yet confession does not silence protest. The book asks whether suffering this great, especially the suffering of children, can be proportionate, and it leaves that question before God rather than answering it for him.

David's adultery and murder are told without excuse. When Nathan confronts him, David confesses plainly, and God forgives him at once. Forgiveness, however, does not undo what his sin set loose. The book traces those consequences through his family with painful honesty, holding together real grace and real cost in a way that resists both cheap forgiveness and despair.

John holds together two truths that are easily pulled apart. Believers still sin, and those who deny it deceive themselves, but the blood of Jesus cleanses and God forgives those who confess (1:7-9). At the same time, the one born of God does not settle into a life of sin, because Christ came to take sin away. Grace is neither excuse nor impossible demand.

The rebuilt temple looked like nothing to those who remembered Solomon's. God promises that its latter glory will surpass the former, because he will fill it with glory. Haggai teaches that God can work through modest beginnings toward purposes far greater than they appear.

themes.title: Sound teaching and a good conscience

entries.body: The letter speaks of sound, literally healthy, teaching, and sets it against speculation that breeds quarrels. Teaching and life are never separated: false teachers have shipwrecked their faith by rejecting a good conscience (1:19), and Timothy will save himself and his hearers by watching both his life and his doctrine (4:16). Truth, in this letter, is meant to make people well.

As in 1 Timothy, sound, healthy teaching is set against empty talk, myths, and quarrels. Elders must hold firmly to the faithful word so that they can encourage believers and refute those who contradict it (1:9).

Every chapter touches the tongue: quick to listen and slow to speak (1:19), empty words to the hungry (2:16), the tongue as a fire (3:6), slander and boasting (4:11-16), grumbling and oaths (5:9-12). For James, speech is the clearest test of whether faith has reached the whole person.

The Galatians received the Spirit by hearing with faith, not by keeping the law (3:2). The Spirit makes them children who cry "Abba, Father" (4:6), and the Spirit, not the law, is the power for a holy life. Freedom in Christ is freedom from slavery, whether to pagan gods or to the law as a means of standing with God, and freedom for loving service.
The Spirit gives life, bears witness that believers are God's children, helps them in weakness, and is the firstfruits of a coming redemption that will reach the whole groaning creation.

In the Old Testament the Spirit came on particular people for particular tasks: judges, kings, prophets. Joel foresees a day when the Spirit is poured out without distinction of age, sex, or social rank, so that sons and daughters, old and young, male and female servants all share in what had been the gift of a few. The promise of Numbers 11:29, Moses's wish that all the LORD's people were prophets, comes into view.

Paul steps in to cover whatever Onesimus owes and writes the pledge in his own hand. The language of accounts, debts, and repayment turns a legal matter into an act of costly friendship. Christians have long heard in it an echo of the substitution at the heart of the gospel.

The church received the word in much affliction (1:6), and Paul reminds them that he warned them trials would come (3:3-4). Their perseverance under pressure is evidence of God's work. The letter does not explain suffering away; it sets it within the pattern of Jesus, the prophets, and the churches in Judea, and within the hope of his coming.

Peter never treats suffering as an accident or a sign that God has abandoned his people. He calls it a testing that refines faith like gold, a share in the sufferings of Christ, and a brief season before glory. He distinguishes suffering for doing good from suffering earned by wrongdoing, and he tells believers to entrust themselves to their faithful Creator.

No other prophet lets us hear so much of his own pain. Jeremiah accuses God of deceiving him, curses the day he was born, and begs for vindication, yet he keeps speaking the word he cannot hold in. The book shows that faithfulness can include lament and protest brought directly to God, and that God answers such prayer, sometimes with comfort and sometimes with a call to stand firm.

Paul writes from prison, the church faces opposition, and Epaphroditus nearly died. The letter does not hide any of this. It sees suffering for Christ as a gift granted to believers (1:29), a sharing in Christ's sufferings (3:10), and it sets all of it within the hope of resurrection and the day of Christ.

themes.title: Suffering and the sovereignty of God

entries.body: Almost every advance in Acts comes through opposition: arrests, beatings, stonings, riots, and a shipwreck. Luke presents none of this as defeat. Persecution scatters the church and so spreads the word; Paul's imprisonment carries him to Rome at the empire's expense. God's purpose stands behind events without making the suffering less real.

Paul is a prisoner, and to be linked to him is costly. Again and again he urges Timothy not to be ashamed and to join him in suffering (1:8; 2:3). Suffering for the gospel is not a sign of failure but the expected path of those who want to live godly lives in Christ Jesus (3:12), and it is endured by the power of God, not by grit.

The visions are honest about persecution: the saints are handed over for a time, the sanctuary is trampled, and the wise fall by sword and flame. Deliverance does not always come before death. The book's final answer is resurrection, the dead awakening to everlasting life or disgrace, and the promise that the faithful will shine like the stars (12:2-3).

The letter's center is Christ's preeminence over everything: creation, the powers, the church, and death. Nothing in heaven or on earth stands outside his authority, and nothing can be added to him. Every warning in the letter flows from this conviction, and so does its confidence.

The first half turns on the rebuilding of the temple and on the two leaders of the community, Joshua the high priest and Zerubbabel the governor from David's line. The Branch will build the temple and bear royal splendor (6:12-13), and the work will succeed by God's Spirit rather than by military power (4:6). The second half turns to shepherds: faithless leaders who fleece the flock, and a shepherd whom the people reject.

The temple is the book's center of gravity. Solomon's building occupies nine chapters, and the kings who follow are judged largely by how they treat it: Asa, Joash, Hezekiah, and Josiah restore and cleanse it, while Ahaz shuts its doors and Manasseh fills it with idols. The Chronicler dwells on the Levites, the singers, the gatekeepers, and the festivals, because for his readers the rebuilt temple and its worship were where their identity as God's people was lived out.

themes.title: They will know that I am the LORD

entries.body: The refrain appears throughout the book, after judgment and after restoration alike. The goal of God's action in history is that Israel and the nations will recognize who he is. God acts for the sake of his name, which means for the truth about himself to be seen.

James opens by telling believers to consider trials an occasion for joy, not because suffering is good in itself but because tested faith produces perseverance, and perseverance leads to maturity. The theme returns at the end with the prophets and Job as examples of patience. James is honest that trials hurt and that people under pressure are tempted to blame God; he insists that God tempts no one and gives only good gifts.

Jeremiah is surrounded by prophets who say what kings and crowds want to hear. The book presses the question of how to tell a true word from a false one, and its answer involves the content of the message (does it call people to repentance?), the prophet's life, and finally whether the word comes to pass. Jeremiah's lonely faithfulness against popular religion is one of the book's central dramas.

Again and again the kings of Judah face a choice between trusting God and trusting military power, foreign alliances, or clever policy. Ahaz chooses Assyria; Hezekiah, in the crisis of 701 BC, prays. The book's verdict is that faith is the only real security, and that everything people lean on in its place, from horses to idols, will fail them.

The word appears five times in the first four verses. Truth is something believers know, something that abides in them and will be with them forever, and something they walk in. It is finally bound to the person of Christ, and so it cannot be separated from what one believes about him.

Beginning with Psalm 1, the collection contrasts the righteous and the wicked, the way that God watches over and the way that perishes. The wisdom psalms (such as 1, 37, 49, 73, and 112) wrestle openly with the fact that the wicked often prosper, and they locate the answer in God's judgment and presence rather than in quick rewards.

Proverbs pictures life as a road with two paths: the way of wisdom and righteousness, which leads to life, and the way of folly and wickedness, which leads to death. Choices that look small, a companion, a loan, a glance, a lie, set a person on one road or the other. The book trains the reader to see where a path ends before stepping onto it.

God uses a left-handed man, a woman, a farmer threshing in a winepress, the son of a prostitute, and a man who breaks nearly every vow he carries. The Spirit of the LORD comes upon them for the task of rescue. The book is clear that this gift of power is not the same as good character, and several judges misuse what God has given. The deliverance is God's, carried out through very human hands.

The ancient world felt surrounded by spiritual forces, rulers, and authorities. Colossians says that these were created through and for Christ (1:16) and that at the cross he disarmed them and made a public spectacle of them (2:15). Believers who have died with Christ are no longer subject to them or to regulations based on them (2:20).

The elder's greatest joy is to hear that his children walk in the truth (verse 4). Truth is not only believed but lived, and in this letter it is lived in faithfulness to strangers and generosity to those who serve.

After Peter's confession, every prediction of the passion is followed by teaching on discipleship: deny yourself, be the servant of all, and follow Jesus to the cross. Mark insists that the Messiah's path runs through suffering and that his followers' path does too. This was not abstract for readers who faced persecution.

Money runs through the letter: leaders must be free of the love of money, false teachers seek profit, and the letter's closing section warns that the love of money is the root of all kinds of evil (6:10). Yet Paul does not condemn the rich; he charges them to be rich in good works and to hope in God, who richly provides all things for us to enjoy (6:17).

Against rivals who measured leaders by eloquence, letters of recommendation, pay, and spiritual experiences, Paul offers a different test: sincerity before God, the changed lives of the people served, faithfulness to the gospel of the crucified Christ, and a willingness to suffer for others. His own converts, he says, are his letter of recommendation.

The book closes by playing on Micah's name: no God is like the one who pardons iniquity, does not retain his anger forever, and delights in loving devotion (7:18). The final ground of hope is God's own character and his oath to Abraham and Jacob.

The question of Jesus' identity runs through the whole book. The disciples ask it after the storm (4:41), Herod wonders about it, and Jesus asks it himself at Caesarea Philippi (8:29). The reader knows the answer from 1:1, and the drama lies in watching the characters struggle toward it, often getting the words right and the meaning wrong.

Solomon receives wisdom as a gift, and it makes him a just judge and a famous king. Yet the wisest man in Israel ends by following other gods. The book's sobering point is that wisdom without continued obedience does not protect a heart from drifting.

Wisdom in James is not cleverness but a way of life that comes as God's gift. It is asked for in prayer (1:5) and known by its fruit: purity, peace, gentleness, mercy, and sincerity (3:17). James contrasts it with an earthly wisdom marked by jealousy and selfish ambition, which produces disorder.

Corinth prized eloquence, knowledge, and status, and the church had carried those values into its life. Paul answers that God has shown his wisdom in a crucified Messiah, a message that looked foolish to Greeks and offensive to Jews. The cross does not only save; it reorders what counts as strength, honor, and wisdom, and Paul applies it to leadership, lawsuits, freedom, and worship.

In chapters 1, 8, and 9, wisdom speaks as a woman who calls in public places, offers life and favor, and was present with God when he made the world. Her rival, Folly, also calls to passers-by. The personification makes the choice concrete and personal: to choose wisdom is to accept an invitation to a relationship, not only to master a set of rules.

The wise men of Babylon, with their omens and dream manuals, fail again and again. Daniel succeeds not because he is cleverer but because God "reveals the deep and hidden things" (2:22). Wisdom in Daniel is both learning and revelation, and in the later chapters it is the calling of the wise to understand the times and to lead many to righteousness.

The key word of the book's program is witness (1:8). The apostles are first of all witnesses of the resurrection, people who saw the risen Jesus and testify to it. Others then bear witness to what they have come to believe, often before hostile courts. The Greek word for witness later came to mean martyr, and in Acts the two ideas already touch: Stephen's witness costs him his life.

Women are prominent throughout Luke: Elizabeth, Mary, and Anna in the birth stories, the women who supported Jesus from their own means (8:1-3), Martha's sister Mary sitting at his feet as a disciple (10:38-42), and the women who witness the cross and first hear of the resurrection. Samaritans, whom many Jews despised, appear as the neighbor in the parable and the one grateful leper among ten. Tax collectors and sinners are welcomed at Jesus' table, which scandalizes his critics.

Against teachers who denied that Jesus Christ came in the flesh, John insists on the physical reality of the incarnation: the life of God was heard, seen, and touched. The cross was a real death in real blood. A Christ who only seemed to be human could not be the atoning sacrifice for sins, and a spirituality that despises the body will soon despise the neighbor.

themes.title: The word of God and obedience

entries.body: Joshua is commanded to keep the Book of the Law in his mouth and meditate on it day and night (1:8), and the book measures success by obedience to what Moses commanded. Victory at Jericho comes through strange obedience rather than military strength, and defeat at Ai comes through one act of disobedience. The book ends with the people choosing to serve the LORD and binding themselves to his law (24:14-27).

themes.title: The word of God rules the community

entries.body: Again and again things are done as it is written in the law of Moses. Ezra himself is introduced as a scribe who studied, practiced, and taught that law (7:10). The book marks a turn in Israel's history toward Scripture as the center of common life, a turn that shaped Judaism and the world into which Jesus was born.

The book begins when the word of the LORD was rare and quickly becomes a story about a prophet through whom God speaks. Samuel anoints kings and rebukes them, and the kings stand or fall by whether they listen. The emphasis is on hearing and obeying, above sacrifice and ritual, which the book treats as worthless when used to manipulate God (as with the ark in chapter 4) or to cover disobedience.

themes.title: The word of the LORD comes true

entries.body: Second Kings is built on prophecy and fulfillment. Elijah's word about Ahaziah, Elisha's about water, food, and war, the old prophecy against Jezebel, the warnings of the prophets against Israel and Judah: each is fulfilled, and the narrator often says so. History in this book is the arena where God's word proves itself, in mercy and in judgment.

Prophets such as Nathan, Ahijah, the man of God from Judah, Elijah, and Micaiah speak for God to kings. What they say comes true, and the narrator notes it. The book presents history as the working out of God's word, and it treats the prophet's lonely faithfulness as more important than royal power.

Few subjects get more attention in Proverbs than the tongue. The book contrasts honest and lying lips, gentle and harsh answers, gossip and discretion, flattery and faithful rebuke. Words build up or tear down a household and a city, and restraint in speech is repeatedly treated as a mark of wisdom.

Waiting for the Lord does not excuse anyone from ordinary work. Paul points to his own labor night and day, reminds the church of his rule that those unwilling to work should not eat, and directs them to deal with the idle firmly but as brothers, not enemies (3:6-15).

Proverbs praises diligence and warns the sluggard, but it also warns against trusting riches, against dishonest gain, and against oppressing the poor. It says that the LORD defends the needy and that kindness to the poor is lending to God. Wealth is a real good in the book, but always a lesser one than wisdom, righteousness, and a good name.

The book is full of songs sung in heaven, and its great conflict is over who will be worshiped: God and the Lamb, or the dragon and the beast. Idolatry in Revelation is political and economic as well as religious, bound up with empire and trade.

The first thing the returnees build is an altar, and the first great project is the temple. The book lingers over sacrifices, feasts, Levites, singers, and the Passover. The community is being rebuilt around the presence and worship of God, and its identity comes from gathering there rather than from a king or a territory.

themes.title: Worship at the house of God

entries.body: More than any other historical book, Chronicles cares about worship: the ark, the altar, the temple site, the Levites who carry and serve, the singers and musicians, the gatekeepers and treasurers. David is remembered less as a warrior than as the founder of Israel's worship. The book teaches that praise, thanksgiving, and ordered service at God's house are the center of a faithful people's life.

Malachi insists that how people worship reveals what they think of God. Blind and lame sacrifices, grudging tithes, and bored priests say that God is not worth the best. The book contrasts that contempt with a coming day when God's name will be great among the nations and pure offerings will be brought in every place.

Israel's shrines were busy and its offerings generous, but God says he hates their feasts and will not listen to their songs (Amos 5:21-23). Amos does not reject worship as such; he rejects worship that is used as a cover for injustice or as a substitute for obedience. The prophets who followed him, and Jesus after them, made the same point.

The verb “walk” marks the letter's practical half: walk worthy of the calling (4:1), no longer as the Gentiles walk (4:17), walk in love (5:2), walk as children of light (5:8), walk wisely (5:15). Christian life is described as a way of walking, a whole manner of conduct, shaped by the new identity God has given rather than by rules alone.

Jerusalem, or Zion, is the city God judges and the city he will restore. Isaiah sees it becoming the place where all nations come to learn God's ways (2:2-4; 60:1-3), so that the calling of Israel turns out to be for the sake of the whole world.
